summary: Future space exploration requires the next generation to understand the complex realities of surviving in deep space environments. We built "Artemis Outpost: Shackleton Ridge", a 2D pixel-art lunar South Pole survival trainer designed specifically for children aged 7–12. Our game addresses the Junior Astronaut Trainer challenge by gamifying actual astronaut training scenarios, forcing players to balance Power, Life Support, and Radiation shielding. The simulation is powered by an independent, dual-track offline data engine utilizing NASA DONKI for space weather events, OSDR for life support constraints, RadLab for galactic cosmic ray benchmarks, and LRO/LCROSS data for lunar water ice extraction. By translating complex scientific datasets into kid-friendly interactive resource trade-offs, we provide an accessible educational tool. Our intended impact is to educate young minds about the physics of the Artemis missions, preparing the junior astronauts of tomorrow.
details:
What it does and how it works Project FutureX is a 2D lunar South Pole survival trainer. Users play as astronauts navigating an isometric outpost with specific zones like the Safe Dome, Plant Farm, and Ice Drill Site. The core loop requires players to manage three primary systems—Power, Life Support, and Shielding. Players must navigate the map to perform daily tasks while responding to environmental hazards like dust buildup and solar flares, ensuring their meters do not drop to critical levels.

Try it in 60 seconds

  1. Launch the game and select a Mission Strategy (e.g., "Power First").
  2. Wait for a "Sun Burp" (solar flare) warning and immediately navigate your astronaut into the water-walled Safe Dome before the countdown timer expires.
  3. Review the post-mission debrief screen to see how your movement and strategy affected the base's physical units (like acute radiation dose and ice extracted).

Benefits and intended impact Children aged 7–12 learn complex orbital mechanics, resource management, and radiation concepts through intuitive gameplay. The immediate feedback loop teaches them why outdoor suits cannot block Solar Particle Events and why lunar dust degrades solar arrays. The realistic next step is expanding the engine to include Mars transit scenarios.

NASA data

  • DONKI: We use historical flare and CME data (e.g., the May 2024 X8.7 flare and Oct 2024 X9.0 flare) to dynamically scale the in-game warning countdown timers and solar-array surge warnings.
  • OSDR & ISS ECLSS: We map the ISS 98% water recovery milestone and nominal cabin pressure metrics to the game's Plant Farm and Sabatier recycler mechanics.
  • RadLab: We integrated the lunar surface Galactic Cosmic Ray (GCR) absorbed dose benchmark (1.36 mSv/day) to drive the live radiation HUD, distinguishing between safe water-walled shelters and exposed glass greenhouse roofs.
  • LRO (Diviner/LOLA) & LCROSS: We use the ~155 kg water vapor measurement from the Cabeus crater plume to set the player's primary rocket fuel extraction goal.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software The project was built using HTML5, React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.

  • Gemini Pro (Google AI Studio): Used for game logic architecture and dataset mapping.
  • VS Code: Used for local environment setup and troubleshooting.
  • Netlify: Used for hosting the game.

What makes it creative Rather than a standard quiz format, the code utilizes a deterministic seeded pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) to build a dynamic event queue (buildDynamicSolQueue). This system injects "ripple hazards"—if a player neglects dust cleaning, low power directly drains the Life Support systems on subsequent days, simulating interconnected mechanical failures.

Factors we considered We prioritized offline accessibility by embedding a 100% offline historical NASA data snapshot, ensuring the game works smoothly for classrooms without risking live API timeouts. We also implemented delta-time clamping (clampDtSeconds) so the solar storm countdowns run at the exact same speed regardless of whether the user's monitor is 30Hz, 60Hz, or 120Hz.

Limitations and next steps Currently, the game relies entirely on an offline snapshot of NASA data. While this ensures stability, it prevents real-time space weather alerts. The primary next step is wiring the data engine to live NASA API endpoints so players can experience real-time telemetry from active solar events.

SI Selections

  • I used SI for code generation (VS Code Cline, Lovable, Gemini Pro)
  • I used SI for data analysis (Gemini Pro used to parse and map the NASA DONKI/OSDR datasets into game logic)
  • Reasoning: Selected based on the use of AI to structure the React logic, design the UI, and map the scientific parameters.
